candidateRows: Divine hiddenness is both an experiential problem and a formal problem of evil that substantially motivates nonbelief.
This move establishes divine hiddenness as a principal challenge to theism and frames the central subject subsequently disputed by both speakers.
The discussion shifts from introductory remarks about debate formats to the substantive question of why a loving God remains hidden from human beings.
Christian revelation requires salvation and knowledge of God to be genuinely available to everyone through ordinary human life.
The response accepts a key premise behind the hiddenness challenge and specifies the universal accessibility commitment that a Catholic account must defend.
Alex O'Connor's claim that divine hiddenness is a major experiential and argumentative problem for belief in God.
After hiddenness is introduced as a problem of evil, Gregory Pine acknowledges that Christian teaching makes knowledge of God broadly available rather than reserved for elites.
The geographic distribution of religious belief is better explained by human sociology than by a God proactively seeking relationship with everyone.
Uneven religious geography is named in the motion, and this move supplies the principal skeptical inference from that evidence to a sociological account of religion.
Gregory Pine's commitment that the Gospel and relationship with God are robustly available throughout ordinary human experience.
Alex O'Connor tests universal accessibility against large geographic disparities in belief and argues that cultural transmission predicts those disparities more naturally.
Divine agency should not be modeled as optimization of a best possible world, because creation expresses divine goodness through limited creaturely natures and agency.
The move challenges an assumed maximizing standard for divine action and supplies the metaphysical framework used to explain limitation, physical evil, and creaturely agency.
Alex O'Connor's inference that religious geography should reflect God's proactive desire to make himself known uniformly across populations.
Gregory Pine reframes the dispute through doctrines of creation and agency, denying that traditional Christianity requires God to instantiate an optimal possible arrangement.
Unequal access to religious experience is unfair when those differences can determine whether a person receives eternal life through no fault of that person.
The argument directly connects divine hiddenness and uneven revelation to salvation, making distributive unfairness rather than mere imperfection the central skeptical objection.
Gregory Pine's rejection of divine optimization and his account of creation as differentiated expressions of divine goodness.
Alex O'Connor grants that demanding the best possible world is mistaken but argues that a personal saving God still appears to distribute decisive evidence unequally.
God is not bound by human equality-based fairness, because creation is gratuitous and differentiated natural gifts can be ordered toward supernatural glory and a harmonious whole.
This is the principal Catholic reply to the unfairness charge, grounding unequal created conditions in divine gratuity and a corporate rather than uniformly distributive purpose.
Alex O'Connor's argument that unequal revelation and its possible consequences for eternal fate make God's conduct unfair.
Gregory Pine distinguishes divine justice from equality among humans and argues that diverse created goods may jointly manifest divine abundance while remaining ordered to God.
A sincere seeker who wants moral truth and communion with God but remains unconvinced cannot fairly bear eternal consequences for involuntary cognitive limitations.
The move articulates the sincere-nonbelief problem in its strongest personal form and links nonvoluntary belief formation directly to potentially eternal stakes.
Gregory Pine's proposal that differentiated created gifts and relations disclose divine abundance within an ordered supernatural whole.
Alex O'Connor asks how theological differentiation addresses a willing seeker who has considered religious arguments yet cannot choose to find them convincing.
Human freedom is limited but meaningful, and divine revelation must be interpreted across a whole time-bound life through patience, endurance, and developing self-understanding.
The answer supplies the principal developmental explanation for present nonbelief, treating a person's current evidential state as one stage within a longer providential history.
Alex O'Connor's case that sincere seekers cannot choose conviction and may remain excluded because of involuntary cognitive limits.
Gregory Pine agrees that beliefs are not freely malleable but argues that people exercise agency in living and interpreting lives whose significance emerges gradually over time.
A providential journey toward belief cannot justify hiddenness when another person's free action can abruptly end the seeker’s life and foreclose redemption.
This move attacks the temporal defense at its load-bearing point by arguing that mortal contingency makes access to redemption arbitrary relative to eternal consequences.
Gregory Pine's claim that revelation and the interpretation of a person's relationship with God unfold patiently across an entire life.
Alex O'Connor argues that creaturely violence can interrupt any proposed path to later conversion, while salvation by counterfactual conversion would undermine the purpose of earthly testing.
Unequal divine gifts can serve an organic communal end in the mystical body, so differentiation need not amount simply to better and worse treatment.
The response directly addresses unequal fortune by interpreting differentiated goods as mutually ordered roles within a personal and communal supernatural whole.
Alex O'Connor's contention that interrupted journeys, unequal access, and eternal stakes render providential conditions arbitrary and trivial.
Gregory Pine answers the arbitrariness objection with Catholic predilection and organic unity, arguing that unequal gifts may be ordered toward others without reducing persons to instruments.
Differences in divine favor do not explain why sincere seekers can remain wholly unable to find a God whom they actively seek.
It isolates the central hiddenness problem as failed reciprocal contact despite divine power, divine willingness, and sincere human seeking.
Pine's appeal to predilection, differentiated gifts, and providential wisdom as an account of unequal access to God.
After Pine presents unequal gifts as parts of an organic providential order, O'Connor argues that this does not address seekers who reach toward God but cannot establish contact.
Salvation remains available through sufficient sequences of grace, while damnation results from a person's free rejection of grace offered by God.
The claim supplies Pine's basic reconciliation of hiddenness and hell with universal divine assistance and morally responsible creaturely agency.
O'Connor's claim that some sincere seekers appear completely excluded despite reaching toward God.
Pine distinguishes circumstances outside a person's control from exercises of freedom and says grace is offered in linked stages that can be accepted or rejected.
A fully informed person could not rationally reject salvation, so unbelief or rejection reflects ignorance or impaired reasoning and cannot fairly warrant eternal hell.
The argument directly contests the freedom-based justification of hell by denying that informed rejection of an infinite good is a rational voluntary option.
Pine's assertion that a person goes to hell by freely rejecting an offered sequence of divine grace.
After establishing Pine's view of hell as eternal conscious suffering, O'Connor argues that knowledgeable rejection is practically incoherent and that mistaken rejection is not culpable.
Only the direct vision of God's essence compels assent; lesser presentations of heaven, hell, miracles, or testimony leave room for voluntary refusal.
This distinction preserves the possibility of responsible rejection even when a person receives powerful evidence about salvation, punishment, or divine action.
O'Connor's argument that full awareness of hell and salvation would make rejection impossible except through nonculpable irrationality.
Pine separates the irresistible vision of God's essence from evidential experiences that remain finite and interpretable under different aspects, allowing attention and choice to matter.
God gives every person sufficient initial grace for conversion, while providence distributes differently explicit forms of testimony within a larger common good.
It is Pine's principal answer to uneven religious geography, asserting universal sufficiency without requiring identical historical or cultural access to revelation.
O'Connor's request for an explanation of the geographical distribution and cultural concentration of religious belief.
Pine argues that divine pedagogy meets people within their historical situations, offers everyone sufficient grace, and permits thicker or thinner testimony within providential care for the whole.
Religious geography imposes radically unequal intellectual and social costs, whereas equal divine concern would lead one to expect comparably accessible revelation worldwide.
The argument turns geographic inequality into comparative evidence, claiming the observed cultural pattern is more expected if religions are human products.
Pine's claim that varied geographic access can still provide universally sufficient grace within God's transcendent providential pedagogy.

O'Connor contrasts neighboring but religiously different upbringings, emphasizes conversion's social burdens, and argues that observed regional variation fits human cultural origins better than equal divine outreach.
Geographic religious inequality cannot be inferred from believer counts alone because the relevant access, obstacles, social effects, and cultural pathways require detailed empirical analysis.
The reply challenges the empirical premise of the geographic argument and maintains that costly conversions demonstrate grace without overriding human volition.
O'Connor's prediction that equal divine concern should produce geographically comparable access and that observed variation favors human religious origins.
Pine says the global comparison is an empirical research problem involving obstacles, institutional effects, minority influence, persecution, and differing voluntary responses to a compelling offer.
If conversion depends on contingent social encounters and trivial choices, salvation becomes arbitrary; if God guarantees those encounters, the appeal to free will is undermined.
The dilemma connects religious geography, providence, and agency, arguing that neither unmanaged contingency nor divine orchestration explains unequal belief without serious cost.
Pine's account of culturally variable pathways to the gospel that remain providential yet do not override human freedom.
O'Connor notes that conversions and deconversions often turn on social contacts, then argues that eternal outcomes precariously dependent on small choices are either arbitrary or divinely determined.
Providence continually supplies opportunities for grace, while fallen human beings can obstruct them because original sin deprived humanity of gifted rectitude without making God culpable.
The response integrates providence, free choice, uneven conversion, and original sin into a single explanation of why grace is abundant yet differently received.
O'Connor's dilemma that contingent conversion is arbitrary but divinely arranged conversion compromises freedom and leaves unequal intervention unexplained.
Pine says opportunities for return occur constantly, compares grace to sunlight obstructed by shutters, and traces human disorder to the freely lost gifts of original justice.

Original sin was humanity's rejection of divinely gifted rectitude and loving dependence, causing the loss of grace, integrated powers, impassibility, and immortality rather than a change of human nature.
The account directly addresses the motion's original-sin component and explains both the primordial act and the condition transmitted to later human beings.
O'Connor's request to identify what the first rational humans did and what consequence of that act is transmitted to their descendants.

Pine describes original justice as gratuitous participation in grace, interprets the fall as self-reliant refusal of that gift, and says humanity consequently inherits the absence of supernatural privileges.
The Genesis account does not plausibly ground culpability or inherited consequences because the original humans appear deceived, morally unprepared, and already prone to disobedience.
This directly challenges the justice and coherence of original sin, inherited suffering, and the claim that humanity freely rejected an initially gracious condition.
Pine's account of the fall as a culpable rejection of loving obedience and a loss of gratuitous original gifts.

After Pine describes fallen humanity as lacking grace and suffering disordered intellect, will, and passions, O'Connor argues that the same susceptibility must already have existed in Eden and undermines culpability.
Genesis should be read mythopoetically as teaching divine and human goodness, free rejection of loving obedience, and shared human and angelic responsibility rather than as a literalistic narrative.
The move supplies the Catholic interpretive framework used to answer the charge that Genesis depicts an implausible deception followed by morally egregious punishment.
O'Connor's contention that Genesis portrays deceived and morally unaware humans being unjustly punished along with their descendants.
O'Connor has argued that Eve lacked the relevant moral knowledge, was deceived by the serpent, and cannot fairly bear responsibility for the suffering subsequently imposed on humanity.
Original sin resembles a landlord imposing severe deprivation on a tenant because an ancestor was deceived into violating a rule, making inherited guilt morally intolerable.
The analogy isolates the alleged injustice of inheriting deprivation or blame from an ancestor and directly contests the moral defensibility of original sin.
Pine's appeal to individual, communal, and angelic responsibility as the theological core of humanity's fallen condition.

Following Pine's mythopoetic interpretation and emphasis on collective responsibility, O'Connor reframes the doctrine through a contemporary landlord-and-tenant analogy designed to test its moral logic.
The fall is better understood as humanity refusing an undeserved palace and choosing an inferior condition, rather than God arbitrarily depriving descendants to punish ancestral guilt.
This reframing distinguishes withdrawal of gratuitous gifts from punitive mistreatment and addresses the central justice objection raised against original sin.
O'Connor's landlord analogy portraying the fall as arbitrary deprivation imposed because of an ancestor's deceived misconduct.
O'Connor has likened inherited fallen conditions to a landlord tormenting a present tenant over an ancestor's violation, arguing that the resulting inherited responsibility is intolerable.
Humanity cannot truthfully be said to have chosen Adam's condition, and even virtual presence in his decision would not establish culpability for a choice produced through deception.
The move challenges both pillars of the proposed defense: collective participation in Adam's choice and the claim that the original decision was sufficiently culpable.
Pine's claim that humanity collectively chose against an unmerited graced condition and thereby accepted life outside the palace.
Pine has replaced the punitive-landlord analogy with a palace freely abandoned by humanity, while acknowledging that explaining humanity's virtual presence in Adam remains difficult.
Original sin is not an inherited corrupt addition but human nature left without gratuitous gifts, with humanity present in Adam by shared nature and able to recover those gifts through salvation.
This is the fullest positive defense of original sin in the chunk, explaining scriptural genre, solidarity in Adam, loss of grace, and eschatological restoration.
O'Connor's objections that neither shared choice nor virtual presence makes descendants culpable and that Adam and Eve themselves were deceived.

After O'Connor disputes collective choice and original culpability, Pine distinguishes literal from literalistic interpretation and develops three Thomistic senses in which humanity is present in Adam.
Even granting personal identification with Adam, deception by a vastly superior evil intelligence would defeat culpability and could not justify condemning either the actor or subsequent generations.
The reply grants a major premise of Pine's solidarity account yet argues that the remaining deception problem independently defeats blame and inherited consequences.
Pine's Thomistic claim that Adam represented shared human nature and that present persons probably would not have chosen differently.
Pine has argued that Adam possessed exemplary gifts, transmitted human nature without transmitting grace, and that lost gifts remain recoverable within the Christian dramatic arc.

The primordial temptation was culpable because it rejected trust in the personal God whose veracity underwrites truth, while the terrible fallout is answered through goods arising from permitted evil and participation in Christ.
The move directly answers the deception analogy, grounds culpability in breached divine trust, and supplies Pine's ultimate theological response to suffering caused by the fall.
O'Connor's argument that deceptive inducement removes culpability even if one grants identification with Adam and his original act.
O'Connor has compared Eve's act to unknowingly reading a blasphemous mistranslation and maintains that deception by the most devious intelligence cannot warrant condemnation of actor or descendants.
O'Connor's sustained theological study, worship attendance, prayer attempts, and openness to religious practice constitute sincere seeking, yet he still perceives no response from God.
The testimony supplies a concrete case of apparently sincere nonbelief, directly bearing on whether divine hiddenness can be explained by insufficient or insincere seeking.
After the original-sin exchange, Pine asks what seeking has looked like for O'Connor and whether his conception of God has developed beyond simplistic characterizations.
The Book of Job appears to depict God inflicting suffering for a wager and then rebuffing the sufferer's request for explanation, which seems inconsistent with a loving and compassionate God.
The move uses a major biblical narrative to challenge whether theistic appeals to deeper questions and human limitations can reconcile severe suffering with divine love.
Pine's appeal to Job as illustrating that divine questioning progressively enlarges human capacity to receive an eventual solution.
After Pine presents Job as a model of transformative questioning, O'Connor argues that the narrative instead makes divine conduct and the denial of explanation morally troubling.

Read canonically, divine questioning can provoke the receptivity needed for revelation, and even profound suffering may belong to a larger providential story that creatures are gradually made capable of perceiving.
This final reply directly connects revelation, dialogical questioning, human formation, and suffering to the debate's central Catholic explanation of apparent divine hiddenness and evil.
O'Connor's objection that Job's divine rebuke and refusal to explain suffering appear incompatible with God's loving and compassionate nature.

Pine answers the Job objection through a canonical reading centered on Christ, arguing that provoked questions and suffering can enlarge the human capacity to receive divine glory within a larger story.
